_comment: Pregnancy episodes. Obstetric care is the single largest reason for hospitalisation in any commercially insured population, so a dataset with no deliveries has a visibly wrong inpatient case mix and cannot support maternal-health, teratogenicity or drug-safety-in-pregnancy work at all. An episode is a structured cadence - prenatal visits on a schedule that intensifies toward term, screening labs in defined gestational windows, a delivery encounter, and postpartum follow-up - which is exactly the shape phenotype algorithms key on. The maternal conditions themselves live in conditions.json flagged assigned_by=pregnancy, so they get vocabulary entries, source codes and legacy codes from the same machinery as every other condition.

fertility._comment: Annual probability that an eligible woman starts a pregnancy, by age band. Roughly tracks US general fertility rates, deliberately a little low at the extremes so small cohorts do not produce implausible outliers.

prenatal_schedule._comment: Gestational weeks at which a routine prenatal visit is expected. The accelerating cadence toward term (monthly, then fortnightly, then weekly) is the standard schedule and is a strong, recognisable signal in encounter data.
prenatal_schedule._p_attend_comment: Incomplete prenatal care is real and clinically meaningful; a 100% attendance rate would be the anomaly.

newborn._comment: Newborns are drawn from the existing cohort rather than minted as extra people, so --patients N still yields exactly N persons. Any person whose birth date falls inside the observation window is a linkage candidate: the generator finds an eligible woman aged 15-49 with no competing delivery and back-fits a pregnancy episode ending on that birth date. The pair is recorded in fact_relationship, which is where OMOP expects mother-child links. Deliveries with no in-cohort infant are still emitted at the population fertility rate - most real mothers' children are not enrolled in the same plan.
